190.title: Pauri 18: countless fools
190.hook: asankh moorakh: countless fools, thieves and liars too, and Nanak calls himself lowly (Japji 18)
190.howItsDone: Pauri 18 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs point to its closing line, in which Guru Nanak calls himself lowly, as a model of humility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asankh, countless: countless devotions, none ranked. Your line was countless, and good. Today, the same word turns around and looks at the other side. Day one hundred ninety.

You know the feeling of reading the news and thinking: people are idiots. The driver who cut you off. The scammer. The politician caught lying. Somebody's comment under a video. It's easy, and weirdly satisfying, to make a list of everyone who's wrong. Pauri 18 makes that list. It's long, and it's harsh. And then, at the very end, the one making the list does something almost nobody does after a list like that. He puts himself on it.
screen: `PEOPLE ARE IDIOTS.` → `A LIST OF EVERYONE WHO'S WRONG.` → `HE PUTS HIMSELF ON IT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Pauri 17 counted the countless devoted. Today Pauri 18 counts the countless who've gone wrong, and it opens: asankh moorakh andh ghor. Countless fools, blind in deep darkness. Then, in paraphrase: countless thieves, and people who live off what isn't theirs. Countless who rule by force and then are gone. Countless who cut throats and kill. Countless who do wrong and keep doing it. Countless liars, wandering around in their lies. Countless slanderers, carrying the weight of it on their heads. It doesn't soften anything. Creation includes all of this, and it's countless too. And then the last line, in the original: naanak neech kahai veechaar. Nanak, the lowly, offers this reflection. Neech means low, lowly. Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh path, closes a list of fools and thieves by calling himself low. Commentators read it a few ways. Some hear pure humility: the one who speaks is no higher than anyone he's described. Some hear something sharper: that the speaker won't pretend he's outside the list. Either way, it takes the sting of superiority out of the whole stanza. Then the refrain: I can't even once be a sacrifice to You. Whatever pleases You is good. You are forever safe, Formless One. So the countless include the saints and the scoundrels. And the voice that names them stands low, among them, not above.
screen: `ASANKH MOORAKH — COUNTLESS FOOLS.` · `THIEVES, TYRANTS, LIARS, SLANDERERS.` · `NAANAK NEECH KAHAI VEECHAAR.` · `LOW, AMONG THEM, NOT ABOVE.` · then, large: `NANAK THE LOWLY.`

segments.voice: Choose one opinion you hold strongly, especially one about other people: who's foolish, who's wrong. Hold it gently. Now ask: what if I'm missing something here? What might I not know? You don't have to drop the opinion. Just let it sit a little lower, a little less sure. Breathe with that. If you feel a need to be right, notice it, and let it soften. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 18. Countless fools, thieves, tyrants and liars, and at the end, Nanak calling himself lowly.
Your line: nanak the lowly. Today, when you catch yourself making a list of who's wrong, add your own name to the bottom, just once. Day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Pauri 19, sound: asankh naav
191.howItsDone: Pauri 19 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; its opening line, asankh naav asankh thaav, is the last of the stanzas built on asankh, countless.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 18, countless fools, and Guru Nanak standing among them. Your line was nanak the lowly. Did you add your own name to a list, just once? Today, the last countless stanza begins. Day one hundred ninety-one.

Think of how many names there are for God, or for whatever people mean by the deepest thing. In your own family, maybe a grandmother used one word and your friend uses another. Walk through any big city and you'll hear dozens, in dozens of languages, whispered in kitchens and sung in buildings on every block. And then think of all the places people have called holy: rivers, mountains, rooms, a spot under one particular tree. Pauri 19 starts right there, with names and places, and it says both are beyond counting.
screen: `SO MANY NAMES.` → `SO MANY HOLY PLACES.` → `BEYOND COUNTING, BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 19 in the original: asankh naav asankh thaav. Four words, two pairs. Asankh you know: countless. Naav, said NAAV, with a long a: names. It's a form of naam, the Name, one of the biggest words in Sikh life. Thaav, THAAV: places. Countless names, countless places. Hear how it rhymes: naav, thaav. The line sounds like two hands clapping in time. And it's the third stanza in a row to lean on asankh. Pauri 17 counted devotions. Pauri 18 counted fools. Now Pauri 19 counts names and places, and then, in paraphrase, it goes further: countless worlds, beyond reach, beyond reach. And then comes a line with a twist. Even to say countless, it says, is to carry a weight on your head. Even the word asankh is too small. Three stanzas built on countless, and then Guru Nanak admits that countless isn't big enough either. It's the same humility as yesterday, turned on language itself. Tomorrow we'll see where the stanza goes next, to letters and words, and why it doesn't give up on them. Today, the sound. Asankh naav, asankh thaav. Say it slowly and it feels like standing in a very large space. Say it quickly and it feels like a heartbeat. The people who recite Japji every morning carry this line with them, the way you'd carry a tune.
screen: `NAAV — NAMES. THAAV — PLACES.` · `A THIRD STANZA OF COUNTLESS.` · `EVEN COUNTLESS IS TOO SMALL.` · `TWO HANDS CLAPPING IN TIME.` · then, large: `ASANKH NAAV.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: asankh naav, asankh thaav. Once slowly, feeling the rhyme land. Then again, a little softer. A third time, almost a whisper. Then let it go silent and sit. If you like, let the words ride quietly on your breath: asankh naav on the in-breath, asankh thaav on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 19. It opens asankh naav, asankh thaav: countless names, countless places, and then says even countless is too small a word.
Your line: asankh naav. Today, when you hear someone name what's sacred to them in a word that isn't yours, let the line play: countless names. Day one hundred ninety-one.

192.title: Pauri 19, meaning: through letters
192.hook: countless names and places; yet through letters we speak the Name and sing His praise (Japji 19)
192.howItsDone: Pauri 19 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikh children learn the Gurmukhi letters, the painti akhar, as their first step toward reading Gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 19. Your line was asankh naav: countless names, and even countless too small a word. Today, the stanza's surprise. Day one hundred ninety-two.

Think of the first word you ever learned to write. Maybe your own name, in giant wobbly letters on the fridge. It's a small miracle. A few shapes of ink, and someone across the room, or across the world, or a hundred years later, can hear you. Yesterday Pauri 19 said even countless is too small a word for creation. You'd expect it to give up on words entirely. It doesn't. It turns and praises the smallest thing we have: the letter.
screen: `YOUR NAME, IN WOBBLY LETTERS.` → `A FEW SHAPES OF INK.` → `THE STANZA PRAISES THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Today's word is akhar: a letter, a written character. Here's the heart of the stanza in the original: akharee naam akharee saalaah. Through letters, the Name. Through letters, praise. Then, in paraphrase: through letters, knowledge and songs and the singing of virtues. Through letters, writing and speaking. Through letters, even what's written on each person's forehead, their destiny, is told. Everything we can say about the sacred comes through these little shapes and sounds. But then a turn: the One who wrote all this has nothing written on His own forehead. No one assigns the Writer a destiny. As He commands, so things are received. As much as He has made, so much is His Name. And without the Name, there is no place at all. So the stanza holds two things together. Words can never contain it; we heard that for four days. And yet words are how we reach toward it. Not in spite of being small, but through being small. This matters in Sikh life. Sikh tradition credits the second Guru, Guru Angad, with shaping the Gurmukhi script, the letters the Guru Granth Sahib is written in. Children learn the letters as a first step toward reading Gurbani. And one more layer: akhar comes from the Sanskrit akshara, which means a letter or a syllable, and also means imperishable, that which doesn't wear away. The letter that can't hold everything is also the thing that lasts. That closes the countless stanzas. Countless devotions, countless fools, countless names. And through letters, the Name.
screen: `AKHAREE NAAM AKHAREE SAALAAH.` · `THE WRITER HAS NO FOREHEAD LINES.` · `SMALL, AND YET THE WAY IN.` · `AKSHARA — IMPERISHABLE.` · then, large: `THROUGH LETTERS, THE NAME.`

segments.voice: If you have paper or a phone nearby, write one word you love. A name, a place, a quality like kindness or home. Write it slowly, one letter at a time, and look at the shapes. Notice how much those few marks carry. If you can't write right now, trace the word with a finger on your knee. Then sit with it, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Akhar. A letter. Through letters, Pauri 19 says, come the Name, praise, knowledge and song; from the Sanskrit akshara, which also means imperishable.
Your line: through letters, the name. Today, write one message slowly and on purpose, and let the letters carry something that matters. Day one hundred ninety-two.

193.title: Pauri 20, sound: bhareeai hath
193.tomorrow: Pauri 20, meaning: what washes the mind
193.howItsDone: Pauri 20 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs recite Japji after bathing at dawn, so its opening picture of washing sits close to the morning itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akhar, the letter, and the end of the countless stanzas. Your line was through letters, the name. Did you write one message slowly, on purpose? Today, Japji comes down to earth. Day one hundred ninety-three.

For four stanzas, Japji has been looking up and out: countless worlds, countless names, a bull holding up the earth. Now, suddenly, it looks down at your hands. Muddy hands after gardening. Sticky hands after a mango. The feeling after a long day when your whole body just wants a shower. It's the most ordinary picture in the world, and Guru Nanak starts a new stanza with it. From the edge of the universe to the kitchen sink, in one breath. Today, the sound of that first line.
screen: `COUNTLESS WORLDS, COUNTLESS NAMES.` → `NOW, YOUR HANDS.` → `FROM THE UNIVERSE TO THE SINK.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 20 in the original: bhareeai hath pair tan deh. Let's take it word by word. Bhareeai, said BHA-ree-ai: when it's filled, when it's covered, when it's soiled. The same verb Punjabis use for filling a glass, here meaning covered in dirt. Hath: hands. Pair: feet. Tan and deh: two words for the body, one after the other, as if to say the whole body, all of it. So: when the hands, the feet, the whole body are covered in dirt. Hear the rhythm. Bhareeai, a long rolling word, then four short ones, hath, pair, tan, deh, like four quick splashes. The next line, in paraphrase, gives the answer everyone knows: pour on water, and the dust comes off. Nothing mysterious. Anyone who's ever washed their hands knows it. That's how the stanza begins, with something so obvious it almost doesn't need saying. And that's the teacher's trick. Start with what everybody already agrees on. Hands get dirty; water cleans them. Then, once you're nodding, move to something you might not have thought about. Tomorrow we'll follow the stanza from the body to the mind, and see what it says washes that. Today, just the sound and the picture. Bhareeai hath: dirty hands. Say it, and look at your own.
screen: `BHAREEAI — FILLED, COVERED, SOILED.` · `HATH, PAIR, TAN, DEH.` · `WATER, AND THE DUST COMES OFF.` · `START WITH WHAT EVERYONE KNOWS.` · then, large: `BHAREEAI HATH.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: bhareeai hath pair tan deh. Once slowly. Then again, and this time, as you say each word, bring your attention to that part of you: hands, feet, the whole body. Then rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and simply feel them for the rest of the sit: warm or cool, heavy or light. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 20. It opens bhareeai hath pair tan deh: when hands, feet and body are soiled, water washes the dust away.
Your line: bhareeai hath. Today, the next time you wash your hands, say the line under your breath while the water runs. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Pauri 20, meaning: what washes the mind
194.hook: water washes dirty hands and soap soiled clothes; a mind soiled by wrong is dyed clean by love of the Name; as you sow, you reap (Japji 20)
194.howItsDone: Pauri 20 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; Sikhs often speak of being dyed in the Name, rang, and quote aape beej aape hee khaahu to say that each person reaps what they sow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 20. Your line was bhareeai hath: dirty hands, and water to wash them. Did the line play while the tap ran? Today, where the stanza goes next. Day one hundred ninety-four.

Some stains come out with water. Some need soap and a good scrub. And some things you did years ago still sit on you like a stain no laundry will lift: the thing you said to your brother, the friend you let down. You can shower three times a day and it's still there at two in the morning. Everyone knows how to clean hands. Almost nobody is sure how to clean that. Pauri 20 walks right up to the question, one step at a time.
screen: `WATER FOR SOME STAINS.` → `SOAP FOR OTHERS.` → `AND THE STAIN AT 2AM?`

segments.voice: Pauri 20 climbs a little ladder. Step one, yesterday's: when hands, feet and body are dirty, water washes the dust off. Step two, in paraphrase: when clothes are soiled, even badly, you apply soap and wash them clean. Step three, and here the stanza turns: when the mind is soiled by wrongdoing, it is washed by the love of the Name. The original has a lovely word there: oh dhopai naavai kai rang. Rang is color, dye. The mind isn't only scrubbed; it's dyed, soaked through in the color of the Name, the way cloth takes on a new color in the vat. In Sikh writing, being dyed in the Name, rang, is a favorite picture of love that goes all the way through. Then the stanza adds something that keeps this from being too easy. Virtuous and sinner, it says, aren't just labels people say. What you do, again and again, is written down and goes with you. And then the line behind today's carry, in the original: aape beej aape hee khaahu. You yourself sow, and you yourself eat. Whatever seed you plant is the harvest you'll live on. Nanak says we come and go by the Hukam, the divine order. So two things stand side by side. The Name can dye even a stained mind clean. And actions still matter; you eat what you plant. Grace and responsibility, in one stanza, and Sikh teachers hold both without letting either one go.
screen: `WATER FOR HANDS, SOAP FOR CLOTHES.` · `THE MIND, DYED IN THE NAME.` · `LABELS AREN'T ENOUGH.` · `AAPE BEEJ AAPE HEE KHAAHU.` · then, large: `AS YOU SOW.`

segments.voice: If you can, go wash your hands now, slowly. Feel the water, the soap, each finger. If you can't get to a sink, rub your palms together slowly, as if washing them. As you do, bring to mind one small thing you'd like to be washed clean of. Don't dwell on it. Just let it be there with the water. Then sit, hands resting, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 20. Water washes hands, soap washes clothes, and the love of the Name dyes the mind clean. And you eat what you sow.
Your line: as you sow. Today, plant one small seed on purpose: a kind word, a finished task, an honest answer, and notice it's yours to reap. Day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: Pauri 21, sound: teerath tap
195.tomorrow: Pauri 21, meaning: when was the world made
195.howItsDone: Pauri 21 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs give daswandh, a tenth of their earnings, and visit gurdwaras such as Harmandir Sahib, while hearing this stanza as a reminder that the inner change matters most.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mind dyed clean in the Name. Your line was as you sow. Did you plant one small seed on purpose? Today, a stanza that opens with five famous good deeds. Day one hundred ninety-five.

Imagine a checklist for being a good person. Go on the big trip to the holy place. Fast, or give something up. Be kind. Give to charity, and give generously. Most people would say that's a solid list. Now imagine someone reading your list, nodding, and saying: those are good. And all together, they're worth about as much as a sesame seed, if what's inside you hasn't changed. Pauri 21 opens with that list, and the sound of it is worth learning first.
screen: `A CHECKLIST FOR BEING GOOD.` → `PILGRIMAGE, FASTING, KINDNESS, GIVING.` → `WORTH A SESAME SEED?`

segments.voice: Here is the opening line in the original: teerath tap daiaa dat daan. Five words, five practices. Teerath, TEE-rath: you know this one from Pauri 6, the holy bathing place where Nanak said he'd bathe only if it pleased the One. Back then it stood alone. Here it leads a whole line. Tap, TUP, rhymes with cup: austerity, self-discipline, the word's root meaning heat. Daiaa: compassion, which we met in the bull stanza. Dat and daan: gifts, giving, charity. Say it and it rolls like a list read out loud: teerath, tap, daiaa, dat, daan. The next line, in paraphrase: if anyone gains honor from these, it's only as much as a sesame seed. Til, the tiny seed. Not nothing. Just small. Now, careful here. The stanza isn't mocking pilgrims or givers, and Sikhs themselves give generously and visit holy places, Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar most of all. It's weighing where the real change happens. And the next lines say where, in paraphrase: the one who has listened, has trusted, and has loved in the mind has bathed at the pilgrimage place within. Hear the words coming back? Listening, suniai. Trusting, mannai. And love. The words of Pauris 8 to 15 come back here, all at once. The real teerath is inside. So today, the sound: teerath tap daiaa dat daan. Five good things, honored, and pointed inward.
screen: `TEERATH — A FORD, A HOLY PLACE.` · `TAP, DAIAA, DAT, DAAN.` · `WORTH A SESAME SEED.` · `THE PILGRIMAGE PLACE WITHIN.` · then, large: `TEERATH TAP.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: teerath tap daiaa dat daan. Slowly, letting each word land, five steps. Say it twice more. Then let it go quiet. For the rest of the sit, think of one good thing you did this week. Don't grade it. Just ask, gently, whether it moved anything inside you, and rest with whatever answer comes, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 21. It opens teerath tap daiaa dat daan: pilgrimage, austerity, compassion, gifts and giving, and points to the pilgrimage place within.
Your line: teerath tap. Today, when you do something good, pause afterward and ask: did it change anything inside? Day one hundred ninety-five.

196.title: Pauri 21, meaning: when was the world made
196.hook: no pandit, qazi or yogi knows the hour creation began; only the Creator knows (Japji 21)
196.howItsDone: Pauri 21 is recited each morning in Japji Sahib; many Sikhs quote its lines on the pandits, qazis and yogis to say that the beginning of creation is known only to the Creator.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 21. Your line was teerath tap: five good deeds, and the pilgrimage place within. Today, the same stanza asks the oldest question there is. Day one hundred ninety-six.

A week's end, so look back. Nanak the lowly, standing among the fools he named. Asankh naav, countless names. Through letters, the Name. Bhareeai hath, dirty hands. As you sow. Teerath tap. Now, a question. A kid at the dinner table asks: when did the world start? What day? What time? The adults look at each other. Someone mentions the Big Bang. Someone else says it depends who you ask. Everybody's guessing. Pauri 21 asks that exact question, very precisely, and then gives an answer that's both humble and bold.
screen: `THE WEEK: LOWLY, LETTERS, SOWING.` → `WHEN DID THE WORLD START?` → `EVERYBODY'S GUESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's how the question is asked, in paraphrase. What was that moment, what was the hour? What lunar day, what day of the week? What season, what month, when the form of the world came to be? It's like filling out a birth certificate for the universe. Then Guru Nanak goes around the room of his day. The pandits, the Hindu scholars, didn't find the time; if they had, it would be written in the Puranas. The qazis, the Muslim judges and scholars, didn't find the moment; if they had, they would have written it down. The yogi doesn't know the day or the weekday. No one knows the season or the month. And then the answer, in the original: jaa kartaa sirathee kau saaje aape jaanai soee. The Maker who shaped creation, He alone knows. Notice how even-handed it is. Pandits, qazis, yogis, the learned people of every group Guru Nanak knew. It doesn't mock any of them. It simply says: this is beyond all of us. The stanza goes on, in paraphrase: how can I speak of it, how praise it, how describe it, how know it? Everyone speaks, each trying to be wiser than the next. Great is the Master, great is His Name. And whoever thinks they're something on their own won't be honored in the end. So the lesson isn't anti-knowledge. Sikhs value learning; Japji itself is full of it. It's about the edge of knowledge, and the honesty to stand there and say: I don't know, and the Maker does.
screen: `WHAT HOUR, WHAT DAY, WHAT MONTH?` · `NO PANDIT, QAZI OR YOGI KNOWS.` · `THE MAKER ALONE KNOWS.` · `THE HONESTY TO SAY I DON'T KNOW.` · then, large: `ONLY THE MAKER KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been pretending to know, or worrying because you don't: how something will turn out, why something happened, what someone else is thinking. Hold it for a moment. Then, quietly, say to yourself: I don't know. Notice what happens in your body when you say it. Some tightness might loosen. Breathe with that, and let not knowing be allowed. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 21. No pandit, qazi or yogi knows the hour the world began. The Maker who shaped creation alone knows.
Your line: only the maker knows. Today, say I don't know out loud, once, about something you really don't, and let that be fine. Day one hundred ninety-six.
